title: Cultivating from the Mind
author: Zhanran
excerpt: From what does one cultivate? This is a great question of deep concern to practitioners. The Essential Method of Sudden Awakening to the Way expounds it brilliantly:

inline.s: As for “sudden” (dùn): it is the sudden removal of deluded thoughts;
As for “awakening” (wù): it is waking to the fact that nothing is obtained.
From what does one cultivate? This is a great question of deep concern to practitioners. The Essential Method of Sudden Awakening to the Way expounds it brilliantly:
“Question: What method does one cultivate in order to attain liberation? Answer: Only the single gate of sudden awakening leads to liberation.
(Question:)
What is sudden awakening? Answer:
As for “sudden,” it is the sudden removal of deluded thoughts; as for “awakening,” it is waking to the fact that nothing is obtained.
[Waking to the fact that nothing is obtained]
The Heart Sutra says:

“Because there is nothing to be attained, the bodhisattva, relying on Prajñā Paramita, has no obstruction in the mind. Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear; being far from all inverted dream-thoughts, he reaches final nirvāṇa.” [Bodhisattva] translated into Chinese as “the enlightened being” (jué yǒu qíng), that is, the bodhisattva. [Prajñā Paramita] To reach the far shore of nirvāṇa by means of prajñā (supreme wisdom). The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “What is meant by paramita? This is a Western [Indian] term; in Chinese it means ‘reaching the other shore.’ Interpreted, it is to be free from arising and ceasing. Clinging to states, arising and ceasing occur, like waves on water — this is called this shore. Free from states, there is no arising and ceasing, like water that flows freely — this is called the other shore, hence the name paramita.” The Diamond Sutra says: “All forms whatsoever are false and vain,” and “To be free from all characteristics is to be called a Buddha.” Therefore Prajñā Paramita also means “supreme wisdom free from the illusory.” [Because there is nothing to be attained, the bodhisattva, relying on Prajñā Paramita, has no obstruction in the mind] Since there is nothing to be attained, there is nothing to be lost. If gain and loss are both absent, what obstruction can there be? The key is truly to realize: nothing to be attained. If the mind is still obstructed, then it is still entangled in the anxiety of gain and the fear of loss, and one must then do the practice by relying on Prajñā Paramita (supreme wisdom free from the illusory).
“Question: From what does one cultivate? Answer: From the root.
(Question:)
What is meant by cultivating from the root? Answer: The mind is the root.
(Question:)

How do we know that the mind is the root? Answer: The Lankavatara Sutra says: “When the mind arises, all dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all dharmas cease.” The Vimalakirti Sutra says: “If you wish to obtain the Pure Land, you must purify your mind; as your mind becomes pure, the Buddha-land becomes pure.” The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching says: “Set the mind upon a single place, and there is nothing that cannot be done.” A sutra says: “The sage seeks the mind and not the Buddha; the fool seeks the Buddha and not the mind. The wise one tames the mind and not the body; the fool tames the body and not the mind.” The Sutra of Buddha Names says: “Transgression arises from the mind and is extinguished from the mind.”
Thus we know that good and evil and all things whatever spring from one's own mind; therefore the mind is the root.
If one seeks liberation, one must first recognize the root; if one does not reach this principle, one wastes toil
(though one may spend effort and labor in vain)

and, seeking in external forms, there is no way that is right. The Chan Gate Sutra says: “Seeking in external forms, though one pass through kalpas, one can never succeed; observing within, in the space of a single thought, one realizes bodhi.””
Therefore the answer to “from what does one cultivate” is:
Cultivate from the mind.
The Heart Sutra tells us how to cultivate from the mind:
rely on Prajñā Paramita
(that is, supreme wisdom free from the illusory)
The sutra says:
“Because there is nothing to be attained, the bodhisattva
(the bodhisattva)
relying on Prajñā Paramita
, has no obstruction in the mind. Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear; far from all inverted dream-thoughts, he reaches final nirvāṇa.”
(For the annotation in full, see
the Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra
What sentient beings see, hear, and perceive are the appearances manifested by each one's own karmic force — the so-called
the wind of conditions stirs the sea of mind; joined with karma, it gives rise to the waves of consciousness.

The root of suffering lies in the habitual reactions of attachment and aversion, grasping and rejecting, that arise from clinging to karmic appearances, and so one ceaselessly creates karma and receives its retribution, transmigrating through birth and death. Practice is to put a stop to these habitual reactions and to sever the root of suffering. The Heart Sutra tells us how to do this and why to do it. Doing so, one is able to be free from suffering: while alive, to ferry across calamity; at the end of life, to end birth and death; until at last one fully realizes the Buddha-fruit.

Among the proverbs there is one called “the bow reflected as a snake in the cup.” It is a true story told by Ying Shao of the Han dynasty: my grandfather Ying Chen, magistrate of Ji County, gave a feast on the summer solstice and presented wine to Du Xuan, his clerk in charge of documents. At the time a red bow hanging on the north wall was reflected in the cup, in the shape of a snake. Du Xuan, startled and disgusted, but not daring to refuse the gift of his superior, forced himself to drink it down. The moment he returned home he felt a piercing pain in his chest and belly, his appetite fell off, his body wasted rapidly, and all manner of treatment had no effect. Later, when Ying Chen went to Du Xuan's home on some business and saw how grave his illness was, he asked the cause. Du Xuan had no choice but to confess that he had sickened from swallowing the snake in the cup. When Ying Chen heard this and went home, he could not for the life of him figure it out — how could a snake be inside a wine cup? Suddenly he caught sight of the bow hanging on the wall, and understood. He thereupon had an attendant fetch Du Xuan in a carriage and once more set out wine in the same place to entertain him. When Du Xuan saw that there was again a snake in the cup, he was greatly alarmed. Ying Chen then told him: this is not a snake; it is the shadow of the bow hanging on the wall. Having moved the position of the cup, the shadow of the bow was no longer seen. Only then did Du Xuan come to understand, his doubts vanished, and his chronic illness was suddenly cured. (See the Comprehensive Meanings of Popular Customs by Ying Shao of the Han dynasty.)
The meaning of this proverb is that people often suffer because of their own illusions. At the same time, the story also shows the great power the mind exerts over the body.

In fact, each one of us lives in an illusory world without knowing it, driven by illusory desires — struggling, suffering, aging, falling ill, and dying; then taking birth again, struggling again, suffering again, aging again, falling ill again, and dying again, and so it turns on without end. The true meaning and mission of life is to free oneself from this vicious circle. The sutra says:
“When the mind arises, all dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all dharmas cease.”

From beginningless eons, sentient beings have taken illusion for truth with this very mind, and so have wandered in birth and death, suffering unceasingly. Now, to leave illusion and return to truth is also entirely a matter of this mind. He who tied the bell must untie it; the sickness of the mind must be cured with the medicine of the mind — and the Heart Sutra is the medicine that releases our minds.
